sections.heading: Remembering what Jesus has already done and what he promised
sections.text: Lord Jesus, Son of God and Son of Man, you came into our flesh for me. You suffered, died, rose from the dead, and went back to the Father for my salvation. Your leaving was not you abandoning me; it was your promise that you will come back. Through your Word, your promises, and the meal you gave your church, you keep putting your death before me until the day I see you.
theological_themes: The incarnation, suffering, resurrection, and ascension of Christ are not isolated events but the saving work of the Lord who will return.
Christ’s ascension is a pledge of his return, not a sign that he has left his people behind.
The Lord’s Supper proclaims Christ’s death while the church waits for his coming.

scripture_references.connection: Jesus speaks of going to prepare a place for his people and returning to take them to himself, which grounds the prayer’s confidence that his departure is not abandonment.
At the ascension, the angels tell the disciples that Jesus will return in the same way he was taken up, connecting his going away directly with the promise of his coming again.
Paul teaches that the Lord’s Supper proclaims the Lord’s death until he comes, which supports the prayer’s link between Christ’s death, the sacraments, and watchful hope.

sections.heading: Not being afraid of the day you return
sections.text: That day does not have to terrify me, because you have bought me back by your death. Your Spirit lives in me. Your love keeps my heart alive. Your Word teaches me how to walk. I have put my trust in you, and you have not failed me. I have waited for you, and my waiting has not been wasted.
theological_themes: Christ’s return is not horror for those who belong to him, because redemption, the Spirit’s presence, divine love, and Scripture give assurance.
Faith in Christ is not misplaced trust; he preserves those who entrust themselves to him.
Christian waiting is active hope, not empty delay.

scripture_references.connection: Paul ties the believer’s hope in Christ’s appearing to the fact that Jesus gave himself to redeem and purify his people, which explains why his return can be welcomed rather than dreaded.
The Spirit assures believers of their adoption and inheritance with Christ, giving a firm basis for confidence as they look toward the future.
Paul expresses confidence that Christ is able to guard what has been entrusted to him, matching the prayer’s confession that trusting Christ is never finally disappointed.

sections.heading: Hoping for the resurrection of my body
sections.text: When you come, you will raise this body from the dust and join body and soul together again. You will do it by your endless power and love. You already hold the seas in place, move the tides, keep the stars where they belong, and give life to every living thing; raising me will not be beyond you. What is perishable in me will be made whole forever. What is mortal will be clothed with life. What is weak, dishonored, and worn down will be raised strong, glorious, and fit for your kingdom.
theological_themes: The Christian hope is bodily resurrection, not escape from creation or the permanent separation of body and soul.
God’s sovereign power over creation assures the believer that resurrection is not impossible for him.
The resurrection body will be transformed from mortality, weakness, and dishonor into immortality, power, and glory.

scripture_references.connection: Paul describes the resurrection body in contrasts of perishability and imperishability, dishonor and glory, weakness and power, directly grounding this section’s hope.
This passage teaches that the mortal must put on immortality, giving biblical shape to the prayer’s confidence in bodily transformation at Christ’s coming.
Paul says that the returning Savior will transform our lowly bodies to be like his glorious body by his power, connecting resurrection hope to Christ’s return and sovereign ability.

sections.heading: Trusting that your people will share your life and victory
sections.text: I can rejoice in your promises now, even before I see them fulfilled. You are the living Head of your people, and you will not leave your body dead in the grave. Past death there will be resurrection. Past resurrection there will be judgment. And for those who are yours, there will be acquittal, peace, and a share in your reign.
theological_themes: Believers can rejoice now in promises that will be fully seen later.
Union with Christ means his life secures the future life of his people.
The last things include resurrection, judgment, vindication in Christ, and participation in his kingdom.

scripture_references.connection: Christ is called the head of the body, the church, and the firstborn from the dead; this supports the prayer’s logic that the living Head guarantees life for his members.
Paul argues that no charge can finally stand against God’s elect because Christ died, was raised, and intercedes, grounding the prayer’s hope of acquittal after judgment.
This passage connects dying and living with Christ with future reigning with him, supporting the prayer’s expectation of dominion shared with Christ.

sections.heading: Asking to be kept watchful and faithful
sections.text: Lord, nothing in my life will be hidden from you. You will deal truly with all of it: the sins of my younger years, the sins no one else saw, the times I misused your kindness, ignored your Word, pushed away faithful correction, and went against my conscience. Let that sober me without driving me away from you. After your judgment, bring me into the peace and rest, the life and service, the work and joy you have prepared for your chosen people. Keep me in this faith. Keep my eyes lifted for Christ’s return.
theological_themes: Final judgment will bring every sin and hidden thing into the light before God.
The believer’s honesty about sin rests alongside confidence in Christ’s mercy and final vindication.
The hope of Christ’s return calls for perseverance, watchfulness, and faithful service until he comes.

scripture_references.connection: Paul teaches that all must appear before the judgment seat of Christ, which grounds the prayer’s sober awareness that every part of life will be dealt with by God.
This passage emphasizes that God will bring every deed, including hidden things, into judgment, fitting the prayer’s naming of secret and conscience-violating sins.
John’s vision includes God’s servants worshiping and reigning in the renewed creation, supporting the prayer’s hope of rest, service, enjoyment, and life after judgment.
John urges believers to abide in Christ so they may have confidence at his appearing, which supports the final request to be kept in faith while looking for Christ’s return.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original assumes a classic Protestant doctrine of final judgment in which believers are truly judged yet finally acquitted in Christ; traditions differ in how they describe the relation between judgment, works, assurance, and justification.

The phrase about the Word, promises, and sacraments reflects a sacramental framework, especially the Lord’s Supper proclaiming Christ’s death until he comes. The adaptation keeps this without expanding into a specific denominational sacramental theology.
The original uses the language of election. The adaptation preserves this as 'chosen people' without trying to resolve debates about predestination or the scope of election.

The reference to 'ministers’ admonitions' reflects a church culture in which pastoral correction was assumed; the adaptation renders this more broadly as 'faithful correction' to preserve the moral point without narrowing it to one historical setting.
significant_interpretive_choices: I understood Christ’s 'departure' as his ascension, not merely his death, because the original moves from incarnation, suffering, resurrection, and ascension to the pledge of return.
I treated the list of bodily contrasts as a paraphrase of 1 Corinthians 15 and kept the concrete hope of bodily resurrection rather than turning it into a general hope of heaven.
I rendered 'the head cannot live if the members are dead' as a union-with-Christ claim: because Christ, the Head, lives, his people will not remain dead.

I kept the original’s searching list of sins but modernized the categories so the prayer remains personally usable while retaining its seriousness about hidden sin, rejected correction, and violated conscience.
